title: The Power That Raised Lazarus
paragraphs:
The Power That Raised Lazarus
The Tomb Was Real. The Death Was Final. But Jesus Was Not Finished.
Four days.
Not four minutes.
Not four hours.
Four days.
Long enough for hope to leave the room.
Long enough for mourners to stop praying for a miracle and start planning for life without the person they loved.
Long enough for the smell of death to replace every memory of life.
Long enough for everyone to believe the story was over.
And that is exactly when Jesus arrived.

If you have ever wondered whether God is too late for your situation, whether your marriage is too broken, your addiction too deep, your mistakes too public, your faith too weak, your future too damaged, then the story of Lazarus was written for you.
Because the same power that walked toward a sealed tomb nearly two thousand years ago is still moving today.
And it still specializes in situations that everyone else has given up on.
The Gospel of John records one of the most breathtaking moments in all of Scripture.
Lazarus was dead.
Not unconscious.
Not sleeping.
Dead.
His sisters Martha and Mary had already buried him.
The Greek text leaves no room for confusion.
John 11:39 records Martha's warning:
"Κύριε, ἤδη ὄζει· τεταρταῖος γάρ ἐστιν."
"Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days."
The word "ὄζει" (ozei) literally means to emit an odor.
Decay had begun.
Death was visibly winning.
Yet Jesus stood before the tomb and spoke words that continue to echo through history:
"ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή."
"I am the resurrection and the life." (John 11:25)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say, "I can provide resurrection."
He did not say, "I know resurrection."
He did not say, "I understand resurrection."
He said, "I AM the resurrection."
Resurrection is not merely something Jesus does.
Resurrection is who He is.
Life is not simply a gift He gives.
Life is His very nature.
This is why every encounter with Jesus changes everything.
Because death cannot permanently coexist with the Author of Life.
And maybe that is the part many of us desperately need to hear.
Some of us have tombs we never speak about.
A dream we buried.
A prayer we stopped praying.
A relationship we stopped fighting for.
A calling we abandoned.
A heart that no longer expects miracles.
We smile in public while quietly carrying cemeteries inside us.
The world sees functioning people.
God sees sealed tombs.
Yet Jesus has never been intimidated by tombs.
Not then.
Not now.
The shortest verse in the Bible may also be one of the most profound.
"Jesus wept." (John 11:35)
In Greek:
"ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς."
Two words.
Infinite meaning.
The Son of God knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
He knew resurrection was moments away.
Yet He still entered the pain of those who were grieving.
This reveals something beautiful about the heart of Christ.
God does not rush past your pain simply because He knows the ending.
He steps into it.
He feels it.
He carries it.
The prophet Isaiah described the Messiah as:
"אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת"
"A man of sorrows." (Isaiah 53:3)
Jesus never minimizes human suffering.
He redeems it.
The tears of Christ prove that compassion is not weakness.
It is divine strength expressed through love.
Then came the command.
The impossible command.
The unreasonable command.
The command that sounded ridiculous to everyone standing nearby.
"Take away the stone."
Before resurrection came obedience.
Before the miracle came movement.
Before life emerged, somebody had to trust Jesus enough to remove what appeared permanent.
How many stones remain in place because we have convinced ourselves nothing can change?
How many people have stopped believing because disappointment became their theology?
How many hearts remain trapped because fear keeps guarding the entrance?
Then Jesus prayed.
And then He shouted:
"Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω!"
"Lazarus, come out!"
The voice that spoke galaxies into existence now spoke into a grave.
And death obeyed.
The same voice that said, "Let there be light" now commanded a dead man to walk.
And Lazarus emerged.
Still wrapped in grave clothes.
Still carrying evidence of where he had been.
But alive.
Can you imagine that moment?
The gasps.
The tears.
The screams.
The disbelief.
One second there was a tomb.
The next second there was a testimony.
That is what Jesus does.
He transforms tombs into testimonies.
He turns endings into beginnings.
He rewrites stories that everyone else assumes are finished.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because Lazarus is not merely a historical figure.
In many ways, Lazarus is all of us.
The Bible teaches that humanity is spiritually dead apart from Christ.
Ephesians 2:1 says:
"And you were dead in your trespasses and sins."
Not sick.
Not struggling.
Dead.
Yet the Gospel is the announcement that Jesus still calls dead things to life.
His voice reaches addicts.
His voice reaches prodigals.
His voice reaches doubters.
His voice reaches broken marriages.
His voice reaches exhausted believers.
His voice reaches those who secretly believe they are beyond saving.
And when Christ calls, death loses its grip.
This is why the resurrection of Lazarus ultimately points beyond Lazarus.
It points to the cross.
It points to the empty tomb.
It points to Jesus Himself.
Because Lazarus would eventually die again.
But Jesus rose never to die again.
The resurrection of Lazarus was a sign.
The resurrection of Christ was the victory.
When Jesus cried from the cross,
"Τετέλεσται"
"It is finished." (John 19:30)
He was declaring that sin's debt had been fully paid.
Three days later the stone was rolled away, not to let Jesus out, but to let the world see that death had been defeated.
The power that raised Lazarus was the same power that raised Christ.
And according to Romans 8:11, that same power now works in believers.
Pause and let that sink in.
The power that conquered a four-day-old grave.
The power that shattered death itself.
The power that rolled away impossible stones.
The power that transformed despair into joy.
Lives in those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Not because we deserve it.
Not because we earned it.
But because grace rewrites everything.
Perhaps today you feel like Martha standing beside a tomb.
Perhaps you are staring at something that appears irreversible.
Perhaps hope smells as distant as life smelled to Lazarus after four days in a grave.
Hear the words of Jesus again:
"Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?" (John 11:40)
Your story is not over while Christ remains on the throne.
The grave never gets the final word.
Jesus does.
The stone never gets the final word.
Jesus does.
Your failures never get the final word.
Jesus does.
Your scandal never gets the final word.
Jesus does.
And because Jesus does, grace always has the last chapter.
Maybe this article found you at exactly the right moment.
Maybe you've been carrying a tomb no one knows about.
Maybe you've been waiting for God to show up.
Maybe you've been wondering whether resurrection is still possible.
The same Jesus who stood outside Lazarus' tomb is standing near your impossible situation today.
And He is still calling people out of darkness and into life.
If this message stirred something inside your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What stone are you asking Jesus to move?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
Together we can help more people encounter Jesus, discover grace, and find life beyond the tomb.
You will also gain access to deeper discipleship content while helping expand a ministry devoted to proclaiming the Gospel faithfully.
Because one day every tomb will surrender to the voice of the King.
